questions.q: What does the woman in red claim to be when she first confronts Horace in the safe room at Shotover Grange?
questions.a: She claims to be the wife of the owner of Shotover Grange, returning unexpectedly to retrieve her jewels before a party. A wrong answer (e.g., "she says she is a police officer" or "she says she is the maid") reveals the student has not read the confrontation scene closely or is confusing her with another character. The error shows a failure to recall the central deception that drives the climax.

questions.q: Why does Horace believe the woman in red is the genuine lady of the house? Give two reasons from the text.
questions.a: Horace believes her because (1) she speaks with effortless authority and knows the safe combination, and (2) the dog Sherry, who usually barks at strangers, obeys her command to "lie down" immediately. A wrong answer that focuses only on her appearance ("she looked rich") or misses the dog's reaction shows the student is not tracking how the writer uses multiple textual details — dialogue, action, and even the dog's behaviour — to build the illusion.

questions.q: If you were Horace, what two specific questions would you ask to test whether the woman in red is truly the lady of the house? Explain why each question would expose her.
questions.a: 1. "What is your husband's full name and where is he right now?" — The real lady would know this instantly; an impostor would hesitate or guess. 2. "Where is the spare key to the safe kept?" — She asked Horace to open the safe claiming she forgot the number; the real owner would likely know where the key is kept. A wrong answer that suggests vague questions ("Are you really the lady?") shows the student cannot apply the skill of designing verification tests based on textual clues.

questions.q: Compare the woman in red's method of theft with Horace's. How does she use psychology rather than physical tools to achieve her goal?
questions.a: Horace relies on meticulous planning, physical tools (gloves, torch, crowbar), and a rigid annual routine. The woman in red uses zero tools: she exploits Horace's fear of prison, his desire to be seen as honourable, his hay fever (she notices it and offers a "cure"), and the dog's trained obedience. She turns his own personality against him. A wrong answer that merely lists their methods without contrasting the psychological vs. physical nature shows the student cannot analyze the deeper character dynamics the writer establishes.

questions.q: Is the woman in red a more successful thief than Horace? Justify your judgment with two pieces of evidence from the story.
questions.a: Yes. Evidence 1: She obtains the jewels without leaving a single fingerprint (Horace's prints are all over the safe). Evidence 2: She walks away free while Horace is arrested within hours. A wrong answer that says "No, because Horace is a professional" reveals the student is evaluating based on reputation or self-image rather than outcome — a common board-exam trap where students confuse the character's self-perception with the text's reality.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the woman in red's perspective on the night of the Shotover Grange heist, revealing her opinion of Horace and her satisfaction with the outcome.
questions.a: A strong entry will show her professional contempt for Horace's predictability ("Amateur. Plans for a year, folds in five minutes"), note the specific weakness she exploited ("His hay fever gave me the opening; his honour did the rest"), and end with cold satisfaction ("Jewels in my bag, his prints on the safe. Perfect."). A poor entry that makes her sound guilty or sympathetic reveals the student has not grasped her ruthless, amoral characterization.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The woman in red is a young, sharp-witted thief who ______ the lady of Shotover Grange, manipulates Horace Danby's fear of prison and desire to appear honourable, and tricks him into opening the safe for her, thereby stealing the jewels herself while leaving Horace to be caught.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a heist movie where the master thief, after months of planning, gets tricked by someone pretending to be the ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the woman in red deceives Horace by citing specific textual evidence (her dialogue, actions, the dog's reaction), analyze her function as a foil to Horace's meticulous but naive criminality, and articulate the irony of a thief outwitting another thief.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a heist movie where the master thief, after months of planning, gets tricked by someone ______ to be the homeowner.
